utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Stewart, if my intuition would tell me that you'd need more time for Davidovic and that you'd be happy with a short extension of time, would that be a good intuition?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That would be a precisely correct intuition, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have time until the 21st of November, if that helps you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm very grateful for that, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Krajisnik, it may have been a bit unclear last week when you initially had asked for time to address us and where it was not immediately clear that you were not only considering it but that you would like to do that, I think last Friday I said that an opportunity would be given to you early next week. To be quite honest with you, I'd forgotten about it yesterday, so the Chamber would like to give you an opportunity now to address the matter that you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank the Trial Chamber for giving me this opportunity to address them. What I'm going to say now I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to reply to me in writing and I will explain why I'm requesting this. And I also would like to ask you to bear with me while I talk about the problems that I have. I don't have any other opportunity to speak. If I have a problem, I have to address my Defence attorney first, then the Registry, and finally you. This is the road that I have taken so far and I have come to you and the first question I have for you is the following: An indictment has arrived from Paris. Actually, an accusation came from Paris. A family accused four persons amongst whom myself. I have addressed the Registry, the Registry got in touch with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I do not know what is the issue you're raising. I'm just asking you whether it's matter that's suitable for open session or not. If not, then we'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly request for all of this to be said in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say straight away I don't wish to cut across Mr. Krajisnik, although I am doing that. There is in fact, although strictly speaking the matter that we think Mr. Krajisnik is going to raise is one in which we don't really act for him, but there is -- and we do say this to the Court, there is one particular reason why we consider that Mr. Krajisnik would be very well advised to go into private session, and I'm happy then to say what that point is. If Mr. Krajisnik and the Trial Chamber then consider that back into -- or of course, the Trial Chamber consider back into open session is a good idea. But I would like, perhaps in case it helps Mr. Krajisnik, to mention what that point is in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, we will go in private session. Not because the matter has to remain in the non-public area, but just in view of what Mr. Stewart just said, and where the Chamber is more or less blind in the matter because we've got no idea on what you're going to raise, and it's easier to go public once you've been in private. You can always inform the public exactly what happened, you can make the transcript public. The other way around is far more difficult and far more risky. So we'll now first turn into private session. And a final decision whether this is a matter that should be in --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Krajisnik, please raise your next point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether my next point has to do with this trial, but I would kindly ask you to bear with me. I have exhausted all possibilities to deal with the issues because I am in Detention Unit. I believe that all the issues I'm going to raise have to do with this trial. The first issue is Mrs. Biljana Plavsic. Mrs. Biljana Plavsic has written a book. She's serving her sentence in Sweden and I'm indicted here in The Hague. She has presented quite a number false facts about the war and about the situation that prevailed during the war. I have been prevented by the Registry and the procedure as such that prevents me to speak publicly. I also do not have any possibility to sue somebody for libel. One of the things that she has written in her book is that during the war in my house there was ammunition that we used to sell to the Muslims --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I checked with my colleagues. First of all, Mr. Krajisnik, this Chamber, although it is aware that the book was published, I mean it was broadly announced in the press about the book, on purpose refrained from reading one single syllable of that book. That's also done in fairness to you. So therefore, the content of the book, if you talk about it at this moment, you would bring something to our attention which you consider to be untrue which is not, and on purpose, not --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You should be aware of the risks of that. Whether or not you could sue her for -- I mean, writing lies in books is, under certain circumstances, not allowed and could be illegal against other persons. We saw also that Mrs. Plavsic is on the list of witnesses presented by your counsel. Of course, the most direct way of gaining knowledge of what Ms. Plavsic remembers from those times is to call her as a witness to -- She'll then have to make a solemn declaration, and if she would then not tell us the truth, she would be liable for contempt, for perjury. So that's a general observation in this respect. If you would like to continue and add a few matters, you may do so, although it's not common, neither is it very appropriate, to discuss the testimony that has not yet been given to this Chamber. So to speculate on what she would say if she was to be called as a witness, or to speculate or draw the attention to the Chamber that she presents lies in books, which books we have not read, is not very common, is not very helpful at this moment. But if there's any matter in this relation, and keeping in mind what I just said you'd like to bring to our attention, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, but I would really, really like to be given the opportunity say everything I had prepared to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know what you have prepared. I ask you to keep in mind what I just said, and I invite you to proceed. So go ahead, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have said that I am unable to speak publicly or dispute anything in the media, and that goes for every prisoner. This woman is a prisoner, and she wrote two books, and all the references to me in those books are simple lies. I'm not scared of a single thing that might be brought to the attention of this Court, because everything can be proven. And I've just mentioned one thing which would be against my interest if it were true. But if you can check it, you'll see that it is not true. The thing is, I have no money to sue, and even when I was a child I never complained about anyone to anyone else. But now apparently Mrs. Plavsic is involved in this kind of conspiracy in the media, trying to make me into a scapegoat for everything. And could I perhaps somehow communicate with her publicly and therefore deny everything. And also, perhaps the Registry could provide the services of a lawyer so that I can sue her for libel, and then you would have a ready-made case, basically, in as far as my credibility is concerned. And I'm grappling with this incredible problem here. Okay, you haven't read the book, but my family back home, my friends, they have been reading these books, and they're living under very difficult circumstances. And when people are poor, they're more gullible. They tend to believe everything. But the thing is, I'm a prisoner; she's a prisoner. So I'm in a situation in which I'm not able to argue in the media, and she's writing things and saying incredible things. And I think Mrs. Plavsic has heard quite a few things of -- from so-called "claras." If you remember, we've had a "clara" in the course of this case. So why doesn't she name any names? And now my third point, if I may. There was a mini-trial here, so to say, regarding my means, financial situation, and it was presided over by Judge Orie, and it was indicated that I have a holiday home and some land. And the authorities received that information, and they destroyed the house. I'm not in a position to do anything. I'm not in a position to go to Sarajevo and sort things out. So I would really like to appeal to the secretariat -- to the Registry, that is, to whoever else who is in charge of this mini-trial, so to say, to come to my assistance, because I have nobody else to appeal to. And something else as well: The witnesses who appeared here before this Court, you mentioned Mr. Davidovic. He said a whole range of things that were published in the media: That I had a fight with Radovan Karadzic, that I stole some money, this, that, and the other. Please, can you get the prosecutors back there in the Republika Srpska to establish the real facts and then either sue Mr. Davidovic or myself. And I mean, the witness was here in this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I do see that you are facing the problems every detainee has in looking after his interests at the other side of the prison walls. As far as Ms. Plavsic is concerned and whether she did write down lies, of course not having read it, I couldn't even think about saying anything about it. I do understand that you are concerned by the public exchange of opinions on what happened and what is a lie and what is not a lie. But be assured that there is nothing to contradict, if she ever presented any lie in books, if what she wrote, what she said is not in evidence, and as I explained before, this Chamber on purpose, the members of this Chamber do on purpose not read these kind of books because we want to be informed about what happened in this courtroom and nowhere else. I also do understand your concern about the media. Again, this is not a trial through the media. Now and then a press publication appears. Also in this trial it has been discussed a couple of times what the value of such press publications is. It has been discussed also now and then what the role of the media -- or at least some evidence has been presented on the role of the media in either deceiving people or establishing what happened. That's a situation of which I fully understand that you don't like it. It's not uncommon, however. In some countries there are prohibition on publishing on matters directly related to trials. In others, such rules do not exist. Whether or not the Registry of this Tribunal has a task in providing you with legal assistance is, first of all, something to decide by the Registry. Our rules until now, as far as I'm aware of but I might not know all the details of the rules on detention situations, provide for assigning counsel in order to defend yourself before this Tribunal and not in any civil matters somewhere else. You have to go through that with the Registry. And whether or not you're entitled to get assistance from the Registry and whether -- and to what extent you would be entitled to get such assistance is, first of all, for the Registry to decide. If there's any decision taken by the Registry which can be reviewed either by the Chamber or the President of this Tribunal, your counsel will certainly know how to assist you in lodging such an appeal. I take it that's directly related to your detention situation, and I therefore take it that you could seek their advice on the matter. The second issue you raised is the mini-trial on your finances. It's more or less the same because it seems to be, if not a civil matter, then perhaps a matter of administrative law in your country. The only thing I would say at this moment, if this changes your personal financial situation in a way which might be of relevance for the position taken at the end of what you called the mini-trial, then of course your counsel will know how to raise the matter, and then I think it's first to be addressed to the Registry, change in financial situation due to circumstances not under your control. But whether or not there is a duty for this Tribunal or the Registry to come to your assistance, to do something against what authorities are doing to property in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I have no opinion about that. Again, the first one to decide on these matters, because they're not directly related to this trial, is the Registrar. And there again, if the Registrar takes any decision which is subject to an appeal or review to the Chamber or the President, counsel will be in a position to tell you how to lodge such an appeal or how to request such a review. The third matter is the testimony of Mr. Davidovic. I do understand, although it's not common nor appropriate to comment in public on his testimony in saying that he lies. Of course when we will evaluate all the evidence, you may draw the attention to what the Defence considers more or less reliable and more or less credible evidence. We'll take that into consideration. But it is published -- if it's published, as you say, then that's one of the effects of a public trial. If newspapers publish on open sessions of this court, even if you would disagree and even if you would consider the evidence given in this court not to be evidence of the truth, then nevertheless the public character of the trial at this stage is of greater importance than your personal disagreement with what has Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. been said. Not publishing on it, if there is no decision which prevents publication of the relevant part of the trial, would seriously damage the public character and, with that, the fairness of this trial. I will not allow you to further enter into the Davidovic matter. If you want to sue Mr. Davidovic for libel, again I would have to discuss that with the other Judges, but halfway a trial starting civil proceedings for telling not the truth in a different court where this Chamber still has to evaluate it is not only uncommon, it would be inappropriate because it would create a kind of a shadow trial somewhere else in a court which has not heard all of the evidence. And one of the things the Chamber would have to consider is whether that should be understood as interference with witnesses. If the Prosecution, unhappy with what the witnesses you are calling, would start any proceedings against your witnesses in a civil court somewhere else in the world, that would really give rise to serious thoughts on whether and how to prevent such a thing to happen. I'm just giving you some general observations in this respect. Is there anything else, Mr. Krajisnik, you would like to raise in -- before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to Biljana Plavsic, just one point of detail that you perhaps did not quite grasp, or maybe it was mistranslated: As any other prisoner, I'm not in a position to communicate publicly with the media. I cannot write a letter to the paper that published all that, this is incorrect and that is untrue, and so on and so forth, because it would mean that I would incur a penalty. And there are people here who had contacted the media and they have incurred penalties already. And now I'd like to move on to my next point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just briefly comment on that. Mr. Krajisnik, first of all, in most systems you would find a difference in regime between those who are detained during and prior to trial. Well, let's say the pre-trial and trial detention, and which are not in a situation where a sentence is enforced. There's usually -- there's a difference in regime. There is another matter, that is that the detention you're in at this moment is governed by the rules in this Tribunal, whereas Mrs. Plavsic, from what I understand, is serving her sentence in Sweden and might be under different rules. The enforcement of sentence in Sweden is under the supervision of this Tribunal according to our rules. I will at least draw the attention of the Registrar to the fact that you expressed serious concerns about the consequences of the difference in regime, and I take it that he'll then consider whether it is any matter to be further pursued with the Swedish authorities and whether or not the Chamber - or this Tribunal because the Chamber is not directly involved in enforcement of sentences - should take any action or should accept the situation as it is. That's in relation to Mrs. Plavsic. Your next point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are aware of the fact that my property in Republika Srpska has been recorded and there are snapshots of all that. And the authorities there have reached a decision on the basis of which those who are unavailable to The Hague Tribunal whilst indicted are not in a position to dispose of their own property. Now, I'm co-owner of a number businesses, and this provision refers only to those who make themselves unavailable to the Tribunal. But authorities at Sokolac simply don't want to listen to this argument and everything is frozen, and it has to do with my ability to co-finance this defence, and it is about my whole life, basically. So why am I addressing the Trial Chamber? Because basically, apparently, these authorities are able to act on the basis of a haphazard decision and I can do nothing about it. Now, my next point: Thanks to you, Your Honours, I have received a computer, a PC. And I contacted my lawyer. I've got a computer in my room at the detention centre. Now, apparently, I'm supposed to return all the computers, and there's a huge amount of data stored in those computers that I need in order to prepare for my defence. Can you perhaps have an exemption for those whose trial is already under way? They are telling me that we will get new computers, but I don't want any new computers. I would like to keep my old one until the end of this trial because all this data is stored on that computer. And I've got two more brief points. I've talked to the Registry - I don't know if you remember - about the conditions for my work and my participation in my own defence. One of the conditions was the place where I spend my time, that is to say my prison cell. And there are lots of materials there, and I asked for a space to put all that stuff, and I'm unable to work properly because this hasn't been sorted. And my last point. I have a disagreement with my lawyer on this one. Whilst my lawyer is behaving in an impeccable way, I have lived up to all my duties with regard to the preparation of this defence, and this was the main reason why you rejected the extension of the trial, and I would just like to appeal to you to allow me to explain to you about all the work and all the preparations that I've made for this case. And could you perhaps put all that in writing, because that would make it easier for me to know how to act. I'm powerless because I'm in your power, basically. I'm not a free man. And thank you very much for your patience. Thank you to all of you; the Trial Chamber, the Prosecution, and my own Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. First of all, whether you can or cannot dispose of your property in your country, if there is any change in circumstances, that could be how easy it is to dispose of any property. I'm not saying it is, but it might be relevant. And then it should be formally put in writing to the Registrar with a request to review its decision on your contribution to the costs of your defence, and then the Registrar will take a decision to see whether it is any change at all, whether the difficulties to dispose of it were not taken into consideration yet, whether it is anything new, and then the Registrar will take a decision on that, and that decision is subject to review by the Chamber. So therefore I would say it's a procedural matter, and we cannot revisit these matters, and we are not the Judges of the behaviour of the authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but to the extent that it has -- that it affects your situation here and the decisions taken in your respect, and if there are any changes, then you may, of course, raise the issue. Second one, data on computer. The Chamber will inquire into the change of computers and will also inquire into the question whether this would result in a substantial loss of data available to you. Mainly data from an old computer can be copied to the new computer, and I do not know whether and for what reasons computers are replaced, but it's something we'll bring to the attention -- your concerns will be brought to the attention, and we'll inquire into the consequences of such a decision. About the space of the materials, it is a matter which at least we'll draw the attention of the Registrar to that fact again. I take it that it has been discussed one or more times. I am not aware of the limits and the reasons why the result is such that you're not satisfied by the decisions taken by the Registry. If it becomes really an issue which would affect the fairness of this trial, then the Chamber will not hesitate to pursue the matter. Until now we'll try to get more information about what keeps you apart from the Registry. I'm afraid I did not fully understand your last point where you said there was no disagreement, that you wanted to explain what work you had to do in the preparation of the trial. It was not perfectly clear to me what the purpose of that exercise would be. If you would like to further explain that, you may do so at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite the contrary. There is a difference, but I don't want to speak on behalf of my Defence team. It's a very broad subject. I just wanted to express my disagreement here, and I don't want to enter into any kind of argument or discussion about it, but at any moment I can prove my own participation. I just wanted to express my disagreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, then that's on the record. There might be some confusion as to participation in preparation of the case and financial contribution, I am not aware, but since you said that you just wanted to express that you disagreed with your counsel in respect of the way you participate in the preparation of the case, and I take it that it relates also to hiring or funding assistance, then at least it is on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're just -- I'm afraid we're temporarily inconvenienced and so is Mr. Krajisnik by the fact that Mr. Karganovic has had to leave court for what I think is a very short time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's do the following: The point was not exactly clear. You said, "I just want to limit myself to expressing my disagreement at this moment." If it needs any further attention, we'll hear from you and most likely after Mr. Karganovic has been available for consultation, both to you and for Mr. Stewart and Mr. Josse. Is there any other issue to be raised at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I wonder if I might simply - and it would be very brief, but just -- just very quickly run through those points, just to make the position clear from the Defence team's point of view. Your Honour has really alluded to this anyway on the question of any change of circumstances. I'm talking about the financial matter. Of course Your Honour is absolutely right: The Defence team, we are aware of the rules, we're aware of the provisions. Of course we monitor it as responsibly as we can, and Mr. Krajisnik knows that he can at any time raise such matters with us, and if there is a case for such an application to the Registry, then of course we will advise him accordingly and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't expect anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, indeed, Your Honour. I wanted to confirm that. Secondly, Your Honour, so far as the question of the computer is concerned, may I say first all that as -- we had discussed this issue with Mr. Krajisnik -- going into any details, the question of loss of data appears to Mr. Krajisnik's Defence team to be a non-issue, that the transmission -- transfer of data from one computer to another is a soluble solution. And with respect, Your Honour, I suggest that Your Honours have many other things to do, that you do not spend your valuable time on that issue because that is a non-issue. The question of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, it takes us exactly three minutes. We'll ask, Is there any problem in transferring data from one computer to another, to the new computer Mr. Krajisnik will receive? If the answer is no, then we have dealt with it in three minutes. And, of course, then the Chamber would wonder why the matter could not be resolved either -- why Mr. Krajisnik seems to be concerned about a non-issue, and it certainly would not help him to draw the attention of the Chamber to serious matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was trying even to save Your Honour three minutes because it is a non-issue, I assure you. There is another issue, though. Your Honour, the position is this: I had in fact this morning drafted a letter. The only reason I have not yet sent it is because I wanted it translated into Serbian for Mr. Krajisnik to see, to Mr. McFadden, who wrote the letter to Mr. Krajisnik in relation to this issue. May I suggest, Your Honour, because I will deal with that extremely quickly and that letter will probably be delivered by hand to the UNDU later today or first thing tomorrow morning. Would Your Honours simply await that letter because I do believe that my letter will explain that issue. Of course it will be addressed to Mr. McFadden, but Your Honours will see what the issue is, and it isn't loss of data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I then understand that you suggest to send the Chamber a copy of that letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I had in fact -- I will say now, Your Honour, I had in the last paragraph of that letter, I had -- I've indicated to Mr. McFadden why I have copied it to Your Honour, and I believe Mr. McFadden will see entirely why I have done and won't have any problems. In fact, I was copying it to Mr. Van de Vliet in the Registry and to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would say now in the public hearing say that Mr. Van de Vliet is invited to share the content of that letter by sending a copy to the Chamber, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have no problem whatever with that, Your Honour. It is a practical matter and Your Honours will see what it is. I make -- who knows what the solution will be to that, Your Honour. So far as the, if I may call it the French matter, Your Honours, as a label, the French matter is concerned, Your Honour can see our position on that. We do see it as our function, of course, to protect and Mr. -- and advise Mr. Krajisnik in relation to anything that has a direct impact on this trial or his detention and to take up the cudgels, if necessary, on his behalf. That's our responsibility. As far as that's concerned, in a sense we can only advise him to take advice in appropriate quarters. That's what any lawyer could do. So far as Mrs. Plavsic is concerned, we, with respect, suggest Your Honour has correctly identified what is the problem, which is that Mrs. Plavsic's freedom of expression is subject to whatever is happening in Sweden; Mr. Krajisnik's freedom of expression is subject to whatever restrictions apply to him here in the United Nations Detention Unit. Perhaps there's a gap, perhaps there's a problem, but Your Honours, on the face of it, it wouldn't appear immediately to be a matter for the jurisdiction of Your Honours. So far as Mr. Davidovic is concerned, we say nothing because the issue is before the court and we have to make the submissions by the 21st of November, and that's the way that we, as Mr. Krajisnik's lawyers, propose to deal with it. On the last point, Your Honour, we have to say that the disagreement with -- which Mr. Krajisnik has expressed, we didn't understand that bit either, and with respect, we still don't quite. We see a disagreement's been registered, we're not sure what it is today, but of course we know what we discussed with Mr. Krajisnik outside court and at the UNDU, but whatever Your Honours heard today in court hasn't -- well, it hasn't assisted us to know any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Finally, before we return to what is at the centre of our attention, that is to further hear the testimony of witnesses, Mr. Krajisnik, there are a few matters which the Chamber feels that it could enquire into and should keep -- should monitor it in a way which would prevent that any unfairness would result from it, but there are many points where the Chamber might not be in a position to do so. That does not mean that the Chamber is blind for the frustration it can cause if you are in a situation where you are limited in your possibilities and where you feel that you would need another situation to go against what you consider to be unfair actions of others. We're not blind for that, but it does not always mean that it is within our jurisdiction to take any action on it. I just want you to understand that if we cannot take action, it's not because we are not aware of what it means to you. Yes. You would like to say one or two more words, but then I would like to conclude. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to thank to all of you for having listened to me. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we'll now proceed with what we're here for, that is to hear the testimony of the witness. That's Mr. Antic. Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, whilst the witness is coming in, I do have a further bundle of materials to provide to the Court. I'd just like to explain that the binder of materials that I've previously provided and the materials I'm providing now, it's not intended that all of the materials that have been provided will be utilised. It's just difficult to anticipate which ones will be utilised and which ones will not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I was a bit very -- Mr. Margetts, since I have drawn your attention to the limited time available and when I said looking at your binder that you come up with even more documents, but I do understand that you'll use them in such a selective way that it doesn't bring you in any problem with the scheduling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: That's my intention, Your Honour, and I hope that's what occurs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is quite confident that you're able to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And just on that matter, at the start of the cross-examination we referred to some minutes of the 64th session of the Presidency, and that appears at tab 9, and I'd like to introduce that document as an exhibit and receive an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, that would be number --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P980, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I also announced that one of the exhibits used with one of the previous witnesses has, by mistake, not been attributed a number and has not been decided upon. We'll not do it at this very moment because Mr. Antic is here now, but just to announce for the parties. Mr. Antic, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony yesterday. I also apologise that you had to wait for quite some time, but we had to deal with some procedural issues. Mr. Margetts will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, yesterday in your examination-in-chief you referred to a stock company by the name of Novi Privrednik. I'd like to play a portion of an intercepted telephone conversation to you and I'd like you to listen to that carefully and pay attention to the references to Novi Privrednik. You'll also note in this portion of this intercepted telephone conversation that there are references to the Ministerial Council, and if you could pay careful attention to those references as well. The telephone conversation that I'd like to play, or the portion of the conversation I'd like to play is referred to at tab 14 of the bundle of documents presented, and if that could be given an exhibit number. If at this stage the copy for the witness could be held and provided to him after I've completed a series of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be P981, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 981. I take it that the booth have been provided with copies of this transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then go the usual way, that is if the -- if the audio goes too quickly, that the translation will continue on the basis of the written transcript and that one of the interpreters checks whether what is said is reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Ones were for, ones were against and since ... No problem, I can arrange it. Just it wouldn't be right if you were to go there without my knowledge, it would seem ridiculous. I'm telling you; I have just consulted Radic and Jaskic. So can we go? No problem, just see how much it is. How many totally irrelevant misunderstandings are there? We have a complete concept of a polycentric development. Therefore, centres must exist, and the centres will be developed more powerfully, Banja Luka and Bileca, Bijeljina and Trebinje, and Sarajevo and Novi Sad, and Nis, and I don't know, and Knin and so on and so forth. So between our concept and the concept of this here, what's its name, your concept, there is no essential difference. Only, not a single move should be made which will not be 100 per cent agreed on. We are not going to do that. We just have to accelerate the constitution of the Serbian government. Clear, and in it we will permit Serbs to organise a little region wherever it's possible in the territories, if they can organise it, let them do it. Last time, you saw it, they agreed at the Assembly of Krajina; who are we as a region in comparison to the Serbian constitution, to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Terrific. That's how they found themselves an executive committee. I see. Somebody attacked there about princedoms. I thought about Eastern Herzegovina more, but it is all the same for each of us. No. I did it like this as a formality. ... Herzegovina? Man, I have 60.000 Serbs in Novo Sarajevo, 60.000, and they made a big coat of arms and things down there. Let's not be that ridiculous. If you're not united, and of course, along with a policy of development and along with a complete autonomy, the autonomy of this ... on Saturday we did more than you can imagine in this Ministerial Council. About this, the retaining of these means and things. We are working on it completely. There isn't -- we will give them a participation fee. What they are doing to Yugoslavia we will do to them. Right, President. Participation fee. How many of us are there? This and this many. How many of us are participating? There are 30 per cent of us, we are participating in the national product with 20 per cent because you did not develop factories in our areas, then you will get 20 per cent for the maintenance of mutual organs and that's it. So there it is ... I think there are no references nor conflicts between us. Absolutely. Only that there is, we want a little, we want it to go a little bit faster. Okay then. But look, there is -- it doesn't arise before drawn. Do you remember the thing about plebiscite? If we had done it then, it wouldn't have been good. But we -- we are preparing it. All these moves you are making are also preparing. Do you know what the problem is, President? For instance, they are grabbing the money from oil, private entrepreneurs. Well, you have to put it ... right now, please. Today we are going to agree it up there, we shall ... Novi Privrednik will put its claw on all of it. No way anyone can get it. You will immediately set up the regional board of Privrednik and then, for instance, out of three litres, three dinars, how much is going to the, what's its name -- Yes. Two will go to you and I will go to ... But, Mr. President, what I would like to know is this: Who will be collecting the republican and federal taxes? Will it be the SDK? That is all done by our minister, by our Ministerial Council. Well, that is -- It's all done by our Ministerial Council, and we shall pay the federal taxes, but as ourselves, and we shall put it to the federal state that it is the -- its duty to protect us and to live with us. That is okay. If the Muslims SDK were to take the money from the taxes for themselves, that would not be okay. That's out of the question. Believe me, it would be a pleasure to see the Ministerial Council, how much these peoples -- people have done, how much each of them has committed themselves and thought it over. Soon there will be a separate SDK and everything will be ... Our primary task is for Milosevic to direct us to the Serbian government, and then, and that we have serious talks with the Serbian government. Today -- are they going today? In that respect you don't have -- Today I'm going to make arrangements for the entire Bosnia. Okay. The 'New Privrednik' will have to have regional boards for Semberija and Doboj, for Northern Bosnia, in Banja Luka for Krajina, in Trebinje for, or in Bileca for Eastern Herzegovina, and in Sarajevo for Romanija. Okay. So there should be regional boards, and they will work to the maximum, but they will have insight in bookkeeping and it should be put ... so that's the -- so that the one who buys it there will be able to buy it third-hand. That's it. Third-hand. Let 'Privrednik's' station pass it twice. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Privrednik's branch office, and let him purchase them and then let him try to export. We will save the guarantees. Let him try to export to Croatia five times. It is most important that 'Privrednik' launders this, which is most important. We have to give a discount of 15 per cent and then whoever wants, can put it in order. No problem. Only don't give it to power lovers, that is, whoever wants authority, and knows what to do will get it, there is no problem. We had here, you know, one shift, isn't it? Yes, yes, it's okay, but one's honour should be kept and ... Well, we are keeping it. We are saving people's faces. I haven't rushed out with a single statement. I just said that the people were tired and they could not do two jobs. That's normal and change is normal. The authorities should be replaceable, and they can come again in two years and so on. In a democratic world it is so, and the problem in communism was that once you replace somebody, nobody ever greets him any more. And one cannot recover any more. And one cannot recover any more. But we don't want this. We can do it. Authorities should be replaceable and it should be done elegantly with no big scenes. It all should be humanists at the end. Also democrats, finally, today we do not like his ideas, and tomorrow they can be excellent and we would call him at once. Therefore there is no problem there. It will be okay up there. Okay. Cheers. Thank you. Call. But let me tell you; concerning the government, I will prepare for the regional 'Privrednik' to be there. You just have to establish as soon as possible the regional 'Privrednik', that is, we are already registered. That requires some work. I don't know who has been consulted in connection with 'Privrednik.' Has Cizmovic been consulted? Well, Cizmovic will get instructions. He is not ... So he will become a member of Privrednik and he will have the priority when we buy something. We cannot say: 'We won't give it to you but we will give it to us,' but that our man has the priority. So, from Privrednik to the member, a member of the Krajina Privrednik. And if this person wants to buy it, he can only get it fourth-hand. Yeah, yeah. So we will be receiving our profit and our commission at three places, so that we'll control the situation. I'll explain it to you on paper when I see you. Somebody should come here and explain to us the situation so that we should work immediately. All right. Today, today we ... have this ... today we -- Radoman Bozovic and we shall finish that. All right. And once we'll have this visit of yours up there, the political one, together with us, or without us, it's all the same, it should simply be for the press. And we should have our pictures taken. All right. There you go. Have a nice day. Thank you, President, you too. Bye."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, first an apology. It was intended that a portion of that intercept would be played. In fact, the whole intercept was played. I think we've only lost time in terms of playing the whole intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's your time, Mr. Margetts. And may I ask, next time, the interpreters on the transcript, and I fully see the problems you are facing, but on the transcript now it's totally unclear who said what. Perhaps, since it's to some extent read and to some extent translated from what is already a transcript, that perhaps we even should take the additional time to say "Karadzic" and then the text and then the other interlocutor, because that would certainly assist in making the transcript more understandable. There's no reason, I would say, to repeat it all at this moment. The transcript is in evidence so everyone who wants to see the better details can consult that. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, do you recognise the voices of the two persons speaking on the intercept?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not paid attention to that. I was paying more attention to the contents of the intercept. I believe that one of the voices was Mr. Karadzic's voice, and as for the other one, I did not recognise it. I don't know how that person normally sounds, how that person normally speaks. I'm not sure who it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, for your information, the other voice has been recognised as that of Vojo Kupresanin from the ARK region. Mr. Antic, you heard the comments of Mr. Karadzic there in respect of Novi Privrednik. Now, Novi Privrednik was a stock company and SDS members were the members of that company; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that only SDS members were its company. The membership in the company was not limited; anybody could have been a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Antic, you say that anyone could have been a member. Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody told me. I think that the membership was not limited, and there was no ban on joining the company if people had interest in that, or ideas. If anybody had an idea for a new venture, a business venture, they could come and join the company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, I think Mr. Margetts is interested to know the facts rather than the legal structure and whether there were any formal obstacles to becoming a shareholder or officer of the company. At the same time, Mr. Margetts, could we deal with it in such a way, because I do not know exactly what the relevance at this moment is, we have heard some evidence about, well, how business transactions now and then went on. It's not the core of this case. Would you please keep that in mind. I'm not saying that you shouldn't ask any questions, but let's not lose ourselves in the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, there was a meeting in Sarajevo on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, I would like to -- do you know who were the shareholders in Privrednik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't. There were quite a few of them, but I don't remember who they were. This was just the beginning. It was a mere idea. It was nothing special. This is my information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The ones you knew that were shareholders, were they SDS members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure that some were, and the others were not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you name us some of the others who were not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember a single name. I know very little about that. I know that the underlying idea behind this was a business idea, a business venture. I can't remember any of the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, there was a meeting in Sarajevo on the 18th of January, 1992, attended by SDS members and members of the business community in Sarajevo wherein the structure and purpose of Novi Privrednik was explained. Did you attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I can't rule out that possibility. I don't remember. I'm not ruling out the possibility that I might have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, as expressed in this telephone conversation, Novi Privrednik was intended to deal in commodities, wasn't it, including oil?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trade in the broadest sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Further, Novi Privrednik was intended to ensure delivery of goods to persons who were members of the company and not those outside the company, and it was intended to be a source of funding for the SDS. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you're not right in saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Well, clearly expressed in the conversation is that concept, and I'll take you to the part of it. If Mr. Antic could be provided with the documents, or alternatively, if he could just be provided with the document at tab 14, which is Exhibit P981. Mr. Antic, I refer you to the second last page of the Serbian transcript of this intercept, and in particular to the comments where Kupresanin asks: "Has Cizmovic been consulted?" And Karadzic says: "Cizmovic will get instructions, and he'll become a member of Privrednik and he'll have the priority when we buy something." He said: "We cannot say we won't give it to you but we'll give it to us, but that our man has the priority. So from Privrednik to the member, a member of the Krajina Privrednik, and if this person wants to buy it, he can get it only fourth-hand." Then Karadzic says: "So we'll be receiving our profit and our commission at three places, so that we'll control the situation." And he says: "I'll explain it to you on paper when I see you." So there's two elements there; that the goods that Privrednik are dealing in are going to be provided from the company to the members; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, it says "our man," here. I don't know what he implied when he said, "our man," or my man, or his man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Antic, I won't seek any further comment from you on that intercept and I'll move to another topic. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're going through to quarter to, five minutes of this session; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we have one and a half hour for this one, so YOU have five to ten minutes left at this moment before the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Antic, Mr. Rajko Dukic, he was the general manager of the Boksit company, which had its headquarters in Milici where the bauxite mine operation was located. However, in 1992, the Boksit company, it was involved in oil trading, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And you had dealings with the Boksit company in your capacity as minister of the economy, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that I had dealings with them. I cooperated with them. I -- I was called upon to give them certain approvals. It was a big company, a market leader, but I wouldn't say I had dealings with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Well, in particular you leased various premises to them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Premises? I remember that we gave the approval to use some technical capacities, some gas pumps, so that they could load and unload oil. Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Antic, that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If we could refer to tab 6D and if the document could be presented to Mr. Antic. And that's in the first binder. And, Your Honour, if this number could be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit P982, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, could you review that contract, in particular just confirm to the Court that that's your signature; and secondly, that this is the contract for the leasing of fuel stations that you were referring to in your previous answer.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature. I'm -- I don't see a problem here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Antic. At this stage I'll just ask you to look for the locations that these petrol stations are located in, and I'll list them: Karakaj, Divic, Drinjaca in Zvornik, and ignoring Sekovici, but Vlasenica and Bratunac. In particular looking at the locations Karakaj, Divic and Drinjaca, are you aware that Muslim civilians were shot dead in those villages only a matter of weeks before you issued this contract to Mr. Dukic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Antic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I've finished with that exhibit, Your Honour. I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn until ten minutes past four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Tieger, I'd like to convey a message from the Chamber to the Prosecutor. There was a complaint during the testimony of Mr. Djordjevic that questions were put in relation to events that were not contained in the 65 ter summary. If there would be any need to revisit that question - I mean, we took similar decisions in respect of the Defence, of course - then you can come back to it. Of course, the Chamber hopes and doesn't expect that there would be any need to recall that witness for that reason only, but if you would have some information or documents which shed a light on it, you could at least request the Chamber to pay further attention to it. And I take it, then, that the message is clear for the Defence. The Prosecution found itself in a similar situation as the Defence now, then, has found itself, when suddenly new things came up which were not in the 65 ter summary, and it's fair to the other party that at least an opportunity will be given to revisit the question, and to what consequences it finally will lead is still something to be decided, but it also means that we would not exclude that from the evidence. Then, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry. It's not -- bear in mind I dealt with Mr. Djordjevic, it's not entirely clear to me. I mean, the complaint came from whom -- who is the complainant and to whom was it directed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the complaint was that some of the events, especially -- I think it was one event of Serbian soldiers being killed, was not in the 65 ter summary although questions were put to the witness in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I see. Your Honour, I can tell you where my problem is. The transcript reads: "I would like to convey a message from the Chamber to the Prosecutor. There was a complaint during the testimony ..." I assumed erroneously that was a complaint by the Chamber to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, a complaint by the Prosecution against the questions put to the witness. If I have not been clear, I thank you at least for clarifying the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I understand now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Margetts, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, as a successful businessman and as the minister for the economy, you're in a perfect position to describe to the Trial Chamber precisely how the monetary system changed in April 1992 in Bosnia-Herzegovina, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not in charge of the Finance Ministry, in order to give you an expert explanation. I can't give you a detailed explanation because this is not something I was closely involved with. All I can say is that the Yugoslav dinar was the official currency, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Well, I'll be completely direct with you, Mr. Antic: That explanation is entirely unsatisfactory although expected by me. It's quite clear that Petra Markovic in the Republika Srpska government had responsibility for the Ministry of Finance. However, it's also very clear in your position in the Ministry of the Economy you had a full comprehension of how it was that the public accounting system in Bosnia-Herzegovina was converted from one that worked from Belgrade through Sarajevo to one that worked from Belgrade through Banja Luka and Sokolac. You are aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a rather complex question, and I would need at least two hours to answer this question and I still wouldn't be in a position to give you a proper and exhaustive answer. Could you be a bit more specific, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: We don't need two hours. It's very, very simple: You were a member of the Ministerial Council, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At what period of time do you have in mind? After -- you mean after the BH government or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Well, there was only one Ministerial Council, and if you want the clarification: You were elected in December 1991, your first meeting was on the 13th of January, 1992, and your second meeting was on the 22nd of January, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember all the dates, but of course I'm familiar. I was elected as minister without portfolio at that time in that Ministerial Council. I wasn't minister for trade and industry. I was only appointed to that post in the month of May by the government of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While you're not asking about whether he was a member of the Ministerial Council is that he now says what positions he held. Is that an answer to your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm content, but due to the lack of time I have, I'll forego receiving answers to all my questions and I'll only insist on answers to the most important ones, if that pleases the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, Mr. Antic, would you please try to answer the questions. If someone asks you whether you're aware of a change in the accounting system, you don't need two hours to say yes or no to that question whether you were aware or not. I mean, only a few details were given, whether it was Belgrade, Sarajevo. Just -- just tell us what you know instead of -- instead of putting questions to Mr. Margetts. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, I'll refer you to Exhibits P65 Treanor 7, tab 78, and P65 Treanor 7, tab 82. They're exhibit -- they're exhibits which are in tabs 12A and 12B of the bundle that you've received today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, the first and the second meetings of the Ministerial Council -- it's not necessary to show Mr. Antic these documents. Apologies if I didn't make that clear. The first and second meetings of the Ministerial Council were attended by Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic, and one of the themes that was introduced at the first meeting and continued on to the second meeting was the dismemberment of the monetary system of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You do recall that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: It was expressed to be "The economic disempowerment of the current authorities in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. I can't remember that, but it may indeed have been said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... it's radically significant, isn't it, because what you're in fact doing is dismembering an entire country and its payment system, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The system of payments dissolved of its own accord, as it were, since it couldn't function because there was a joint SDK service which was rather specific for that country and does not exist in any other countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, you know that's a blatant untruth, don't you? The truth is it didn't just spontaneously resolve at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And I refer Your Honours to the speech of Momcilo Krajisnik, which you'll see at tab 11, which was a speech he delivered in the Assembly session in February 1992. And if I could have the exhibit number for that speech, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P983, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- the Defence is -- asks through Your Honours is this going to be a question rather than just a reference to this material?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, may I take it that you'll confront the witness with the content of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik stated in February 1992 to the persons present at the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- no need to show to the witness this document, thank you. "As far as the SDK is concerned, it will remain in Sarajevo. Trebinje and Bijeljina and every other existing branch in Bosnia and Herzegovina can be linked directly to Belgrade at any moment. So, that branch and all those sub-branches that this branch encompasses can be directly ripped from the system of this present SDK. I would, therefore, like to ask for a compromise. Namely, that the branch designated in Banja Luka can at any time be separated and linked to Belgrade. Can we accept it like that?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Trial Chamber has the document, Mr. Margetts has the document. The witness, who is the person under cross-examination, should, with respect, also have the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends. I take it Mr. Margetts is just confronting him with part of it, where it's for the Chamber more important.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, with respect, the witness -- the witness is then -- it may not be a long passage, but the witness is having to remember the question. He really ought to be able to refresh himself by having the same document in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the passage just read to him be put in front of him so he can consult it if he answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm happy to have the question struck. The fact is that I certainly would like the document to be introduced because it forms the basis for my question. However, I'm happy to proceed without the cumbersome procedure of the document being presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But now you've read it. Next time, Mr. Margetts, make up your mind before you read it. So now the witness gets in front of him -- what page is it? ERN number in the -- let me just --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: It's tab 11, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and then it would be which portion?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The portion in English is at the top. The pages, unfortunately, are not numbered, but it is at the top of the second last page in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's where it reads, "We can put the National Bank in --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And it's at page 0279421 of the Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Semi-last page, Madam Usher, of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And the last full paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Antic, you are fully aware that that was the policy of Momcilo Krajisnik. He had in fact met with you in your capacity as a member of the Ministerial Council and he had expressed that view to you, hadn't he?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall that meeting. I don't know whether there were more such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, I think you've misunderstood my question. My question was that that opinion and that policy was expressed to you, not specifically focusing on whether you remember the specific meeting. So in the period of January and February of 1992, did either Momcilo Krajisnik, Radovan Karadzic, or representatives of those two persons express that view to you, that the system, payment system in Bosnia-Herzegovina would be ripped apart and Banja Luka would be attached to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, you've seen in the telephone intercept that was played to you that Radovan Karadzic said to Mr. Kupresanin that "It would be a pleasure to see the Ministerial Council how much these people have done. How much each of them has committed themselves and thought it over. Soon there will be a separate SDK and everything will be --" and he was cut off by Mr. Kupresanin, who said, "Our primary task is for Milosevic to direct Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. us to the Serbian government and that we have serious talks with the Serbian government." Now, that's entirely consistent with the comments of Mr. Krajisnik that you've just read, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've read this and I've read the other text as well, but it's just that back then I wasn't really aware of any of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: It's clear from that text that the Ministerial Council is the primary body that's going to achieve that end, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know that the Ministerial Council did anything about that. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Antic, we're in receipt of an intercepted telephone conversation between Momcilo Krajisnik and Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's at tab 7 of the binder you received yesterday. If we could receive -- if we could have an exhibit number and that could be presented to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P984, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, if you could read the transcript of that conversation. The parts of the conversation that I'd like to emphasise with you, approximately the fourth line. Karadzic says to Krajisnik: "Milosevic said that we are to install a man up there, to have an office up there all the time." And further on in the text, Karadzic again says to Krajisnik: "The president said that up there in the ministry of commerce one office should be opened as a representative body." And further on in the text, Radovan asks Momcilo Krajisnik: "Would this Bozo Antic be okay?" And Krajisnik says: "He would be great. Well, let's sit with him. Screw it." So if you could take your time to read that conversation, and if you could tell the Trial Chamber precisely what it was that Momcilo Krajisnik and Radovan Karadzic had in mind for you at February 1992, please do so.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that this is the first I've heard of this idea of it being debated. Neither one of them ever raised it with me in any shape or form.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Antic. Mr. Antic, your presence in Belgrade really may have had something to do with your family matters, but the primary reason you were in Belgrade was to assist in the setting up of this new payment system, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You must have confused me with somebody else. I've never been to Belgrade in any official capacity, on any government business, and especially not with regard to the accounting service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Antic, I'd like to turn to another topic. We saw yesterday that there was a specification of the areas that were within your portfolio as the minister for the economy in the guidelines that were provided by the Presidency, or the War Presidency. Included in that specification was a responsibility that you had in regard to war booty. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, as at the end of May, the start of June 1992, there was substantial abandoned property on the territory of Republika Srpska; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And there were various regulations put in place with regard to the collection of that abandoned property and the placement of that in the commodity reserves of Republika Srpska; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could refer to tab 6A, and that is a decree on the mandatory delivery of war booty and booty acquired by other means to the republic's emergency reserves. Could it please have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P985, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, could you please look at the Official Gazette of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, number 8, and decision 177, which is Exhibit P985, and could you confirm that this is the decree on war booty that was issued by the Government of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And could you pay special attention to Article 1 and confirm that that was the definition of the war booty that constituted the subject of this decree.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you specify the question, please? What is your actual question with reference to Article 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Antic. I was moving to that question. The question is as follows: We've referred to the abandoned property on the territory of Republika Srpska, and that abandoned property included those matters referred to in Article 1, movable property and assets, commodities, technical equipment, vehicles and equipment, cash, foreign currency, gold, other precious metals and valuables. That's correct, isn't it? If you could --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And -- and the reason that all of that material had been abandoned is that people had left their homes on various parts of the territory; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not about real estate. It is about businesses. It is just about businesses, not about any form of private property.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, there's no distinction in this decree between private or public property, is there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not specified. What is specified here is that commissions would be established that would specify things and provide directions, and you can see this in the following articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: That's correct, but the fact is that the property that you were collecting included cash, foreign currency, gold, and other precious metals. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The idea was that if there was a company that had such precious materials or money or gold, then it would apply to that company, not to any private individuals. That was the idea behind this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, can you give any reasonable explanation as to why that important part of the definition of the property was left out of this decree?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, this was not done on purpose, and the goal was to prevent illegal looting or theft, to prevent people from wilfully taking things away. We wanted to place things under our control, to register things, to be aware of what belongs to whom, and one day, when the time was right, to be able to tell what belongs to whom. This was the underlying idea. Why this was omitted must have been a technical mistake, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Antic, with respect, that idea is very different to your first idea. The accurate collection -- the collection and accurate recording of what property had been abandoned is very different to the restrictive idea of only collecting property from businesses. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber, if you take those two ideas together, why it was that you considered the protection of some property to be important and not other property?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We believed that the property of individuals should be protected by the police, whereas the property of companies should be protected by us. When it came to the property of actual persons, we believed that it was the task of the police to protect it. That's how we saw it, and that's what we did, because we did not have any instruments at your disposal to deal with individual cases, and there were hundreds of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Can you explain why it was that people who had accumulated property in their companies, as you seek to limit this to, although it's not apparent on the document, why people who had left their cash in companies would have abandoned their cash?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In hypothetical terms why this was the case: If, for instance, they fled or left for certain reasons and if they hadn't taken that because they considered that theft, that's the only reason why somebody would have left things behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And that's correct, the cash -- people would only leave cash, foreign currency, gold, or other precious metals behind if they were fleeing an imminent danger. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only in those cases. For example, in my case, I left my things in my company although I did not flee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: It's the case in preparing this decree you were aware that a lot of people had abandoned their property to save their lives, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking only about companies. I don't know anything about the reasons of individuals. This was not my concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Well, companies, certainly a corporate form for certain technical legal reasons, but companies consist of people as well. So within the confines of your answer, it's the fact that the people who were in those companies had abandoned those companies urgently to save their lives, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, the republic's emergency reserves were administered by the Ministry of Defence, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The emergency reserves were in the hands of the directorate for the emergency reserves. It was a civilian body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And they were frequently depleted, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And it wasn't the case that in the emergency reserves you held things on trust. In fact, what you did is you collected the war booty to renew those republics -- those emergency reserves and then you expended those emergency reserves, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Absolutely not. Emergency reserves were created through a system of building up emergency reserves, and the equipment and commodities that could be construed as war booty were also placed into the emergency reserves, just to be under control and to be recorded. They were not collected for that reason in the first place. Once they existed, they were placed among the emergency reserves to be under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You're aware of decisions of municipalities and regions wherein abandoned property immediately became the property of the local Municipal Assembly and was expended by the Assembly, are you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our regulations, everything was under the control of the republican directorate for emergency reserves. I can't remember any specific case, but I know that there were such cases, but this was against the law. They should have been placed under the control of the directorate for emergency reserves. And if there was a need, the directorate could distribute those goods or sell to -- to whomever they deemed necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Antic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And thank you, Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
