utterances.text: I would have one additional question, Mr. Antic, in view of the last questions put to you by Mr. Margetts. What does it mean, "emergency reserve"?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were commodity reserves, not so much emergency reserves, which means that in any given moment the state has to have at its disposal certain quantities of food and bare necessities; fuel and so on and so forth, in case the regular supplies become scarce. When that happens, the supply goes from the commodity reserves, then when the supply flows become regular again, the commodity reserves are replenished from the regular supplies, and that's how the commodity reserves function. It is not so much the matter of those reserves being emergency reserves. They're just commodity reserves for certain cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I understand that such a reserve is to be used? I mean, what's in that reserve can be used whenever there's need to use it, wouldn't it? Isn't that the meaning of what a reserve is?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want foreign currency to be delivered to a commission and then send it to the republic reserves, wouldn't you then use the reserve if need be?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Such reserves, which do not exist in practice, they're only hypothetical reserves, would be placed under the control of the national bank. This has been provided for by the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not what this decree says, isn't it? It says that everything should be stored, taken care of, and then be delivered to the republic's emergency reserves. That's what the decree says, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, that particular article of the decree does have a next section, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm aware that Article 5 doesn't stop at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I was looking at the last but one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was talking about Article 5, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I draw your attention to Article 1, Your Honour, because the question that Your Honour just put to the witness just now, which ties very closely to the first bit of Article 1, I was just suggesting one ought to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I read it -- just to avoid whatever confusion, I was thinking of Article 5, which says: "After the transfer --" that is the transfer of the goods described in accordance with Article 4 "-- the municipal commission must provide adequate storage and care of the delivered movable property and assets pending their delivery to the republic's emergency reserves."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will, with respect, persist with my observation, because the witness did refer to the national bank in an answer, and when one looks at the exchange of questions and answers in the last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do see it. I think I made a mistake. It's the risk of -- thank you for drawing my attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm very much obliged, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have overlooked that, and that's one of the risks of being confronted with these kind of documents only just before questions are put in relation to that. Then if they are put in the -- the foreign currency, if that's put in the national bank, was it registered as in a similar way as in Article 4? That means, that it was registered who was the owner of the -- this currency, how it was obtained by the one who delivered it.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. Probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you guide us as to where to find such registers of delivery of foreign currency to the national bank and then the registration of all the information as we find it in Article 4 that should be recorded; how those people had got it, who were the initial owners?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that. You have to look at the documents of the national bank to find that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware of any -- of any system where the initial owners were -- could receive their -- for example, their foreign currency back? Was there a practice where people could go to the national bank and say, "I'd like to have a look in the registers to see whether the one who stole my money, or who received my money, I'd like to have it back"?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how this might have functioned, and any answer on my part would be pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, about what ended up in the republic's emergency reserves, of which you said they were not emergency reserves but just reserves, for example, vehicles delivered to that reserves, are you aware of claims later on? People said, "Someone must have delivered my car to the commission," and then it must have been delivered to the emergency reserves, or were these cars just used?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I did not understand your question. Could you please be more specific?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about private vehicles? This is what I would like you to clarify for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm talking about any vehicle. Citizens might have understood this to be for everything they had taken or received. Are you aware, under this decree, when equipment, when vehicles, whatever was delivered to the commission and was described precisely and then delivered to the republic emergency services -- reserves, whether it was then used? I mean, a car. You can use a car. Then it -- it's not in the reserve any more.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see. Of course there were cases when things were entered into the reserves and subsequently those same things were used from the reserves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is that a measure to protect the initial owner or is that a measure which suits well the needs of the republic at that moment?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those things were used to serve the needs of certain bodies. In any case, this was the road to take in order to see who the owner was once the conditions for that were in place. In other words, after the war, every owner of such property could find out where the property was, whether it was lost; and if it was lost, to seek compensation in respect of that property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any numbers of how much compensation was paid to those who were -- who lost their movable property?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't answer this because I don't know. I believe that the number is very low. And in my specific case, I don't even know who to address in order to restore what I lost. This is in my specific case. Not to this very day do I know who to talk to in order to get compensated for what I myself lost during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You think that the number is very low. What makes you believe that the number is very low? Did you not think this system to be very effective in compensating people for property they -- for movable property they had lost?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply put, I don't have any information about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just prior to the opportunity for Defence counsel to re-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I do have a document that I'd like to present to the Trial Chamber. It's a list of the members of Novi Privrednik. It is relevant to this witness's evidence, although I don't think it is a document that needs to be presented to the witness. So if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a contextual for the -- where the witness had difficulties in identifying who are members or shareholders, I don't know exactly how to understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The witness expressed a view as to who composed the membership of the stock company, and this is a contemporaneous document that sets out that membership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we wouldn't mind having a look at it sometime. Perhaps we could be supplied with the document and then we could consider it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't mean this second. I -- I mean, take it away with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And at this moment I must observe that it's in Cyrillic and we don't have a translation, so it may be useful for Mr. Krajisnik to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We regard that as a minor problem, Your Honour, but nevertheless we wish to take it away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: But on the plus side, it is a list of names and -- addresses and numbers in terms of specifying the shareholding of the individuals named, so -- so, Your Honour, pending the Defence's response, I don't know whether it would be appropriate for that to be given an exhibit number or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's wait for a second. Perhaps Mr. Krajisnik could have a look at it. I don't know whether he has any knowledge about membership or shareholdership, but at least give him an opportunity. Mr. Margetts, I notice to start with that there seems not to be any date on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I cannot find a date on it or any contextualising date within it. I am aware that there are various documents that were seized from a specific location related to this topic, and it is possible that we would have a contextualising document which would assist in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you assist the Defence in telling where you -- where you found this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or where this document was found. I don't expect you found it personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: These documents were seized from the Holiday Inn in Sarajevo, I believe in April 1992, by the Bosnian authorities. I believe it was from the registered head office of Novi Privrednik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And if it's of assistance, it's -- my understanding is that this document will be dated contextually to around December 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll hear from Mr. Stewart if there is any objection, and if he can't give that answer now, he is at least invited now to ask any further questions to the witness if there's any need.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is in fact more than one document which has come up in the cross-examination of this witness that the Defence would like to give consideration to. The question we -- we often deal with the question of admission of documents at the end of a witness's evidence and we do occasionally, or Your Honours do occasionally then deal with it the next day or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just wondered if you could at this moment. If not -- whether you could at this moment say whether there would be any -- I would say initial objection against admission, because then it would be assigned a number. And I said that if you could not, that you were invited to put any question to the witness, not specifically in relation to this document but in re-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour, thank you. I just have probably two questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Antic, you just referred a few minutes ago to what you had lost during the war. What did you lose during the war?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My business assets, everything that had to do with my company; the production materials, ready-made finished products, the premises, altogether worth over 3 billion German marks at the time, and I still know where those things are, or at least where they were at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Have you ever had any of that property back?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises, the value was 3 million.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The interpretation of the answer of the witness to the question that he never had it back, and the 3 billion turns out to be 3 million.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, that's just the correction on the transcript comes between the question and the answer, as Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Antic, you would have wished to have it had at the time and not had lost it, but it is a number which is not correct. Three million. Yes, please proceed, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you aware of any -- any politician in any other part of former Yugoslavia at the time of the war who had exactly the same name as you, first and last name?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first and last name, Bozidar Antic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, another Bozidar -- well, you put it slightly -- Bozidar Antic is your name, as I say it. And who was he?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a man who was either deputy minister or minister of trade of the Federal Republic of Serbia or the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I don't know whether he was at -- whether he was at the republican or at the federal level. I believe that he was at the level of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No more questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for a better understanding of both, the last question and the answer, is there anywhere in the documents where we've found until now the name and the first name of this witness? Is there any risk of confusion or is just for future events that you say whenever you find the name of Bozidar Antic it might well be the other one? Is it on any of the -- because -- because I have to go through this -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour. There is a risk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but could you -- could you materialise? Where should we be, in view of any document presented, be cautious not to draw conclusions too easily?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, sorry, I'm afraid I can only answer that by saying that of course in many instances it will be absolutely plain from the context or the nature of the document that it is this Mr. Bozidar Antic. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any point where it's -- you consider it not to be absolutely plain?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'd like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you answer the question at later stage, it would be fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I can't point to anything right now, Your Honour, but I brought out, if you like, the -- well, I brought out the question and answer, and where it leads on future perusal of any document is an open question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, I have also a question for you. In one of the questions you did put to the witness you suggested that he went to Belgrade, not to accompany his wife and children to go there but he actually went there for a totally different reason. The witness denied that quite strongly. Is there anything you know about, apart from what you've shown us, that would support your suggestion that that was the real reason for going to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's nothing that directly names this witness as being a representative placed in the ministry in Belgrade. The suggestion from us was based upon an extensive reading of various intercepts as well as analysis of the government minutes. The intercepts make it clear that that's in fact what occurred, and the government minutes subsequently confirm that there was economic Presidency in the Chamber of Commerce -- or in the ministry in Belgrade, and I can provide those references to Your Honour. So it was a process of elimination that was the basis for that question, and the manner of the witness's presentation of an alternative explanation in his evidence led us to be curious as to whether that was in fact the correct reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And may I take it that if you say the extensive reading of various intercepts, that -- are these intercepts that are available to the Chamber? I mean, you might have a lot of intercepts more than we received in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: That is the case. These are not intercepts that are in evidence, but -- well, I can't say that categorically. Some of them may in fact be in evidence, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- systematically verified whether they are in evidence. That also means that the Chamber cannot on the basis of that material form itself an opinion on, well, reliability and credibility in this respect because it relies on material which is not available to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think the Prosecution would concede that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have one question for you. You said all kinds of rumours of you yourself taking advantage from the privatisation and the criticism was totally incorrect. Who became the effective owners of the company that was privatised and -- that is the company you were on the board of? Who finally became the owners of that company?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The employed staff. Amongst them I myself, and I got a symbolic percentage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what was the symbolic percentage you received?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, but about 1 per cent, and in the end I left it to them that percentage that was mine. After the war, when the payments were being made, I did not even ask for that payment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How many people were employed in that company?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was a manager, 800.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many got a share of the -- you said it was the -- finally the owners were the employed staff. Did you all become owners? How many owners did the company have after the privatisation?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody, more or less. I actually left, so I don't know what happened later, but in that initial stage that I was in charge of, more or less everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that would be 800 people becoming the owners of that company. What did they have to pay for their ownership?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the law at the time, they didn't have to pay anything. It was just that the value of the company was divided up according to the criteria enshrined in the law passed by the then Prime Minister Ante Markovic, and then everybody got a certain percentage. So every single employee got a percentage according to that set of criteria. And so in case the company was to be sold or whatever else happened, they would participate in the proceeds. So it was a kind of workers share ownership. It was slightly different from what you have today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what now exactly was the criticism? Because I do understand that everyone got a part of it. What now exactly was the criticism? I mean, in this system, all those who worked in the company had the advantage or the profit of becoming owner of a company in which they were employed previously.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a fabrication, because of course you have to say something in order to fire a person, and the public opinion is likely to believe that there is some shady dealing or some kind of crime, et cetera. So that's the only reason. It was just the way of bandying about my name and being able to pin something on me. So there was no real criticism. It was all invented. It was all a fabrication, and they were all aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What exactly was fabricated? I see that you say yourself that you got 1 per cent, where, I would say, on the average, every employee would get one share out of 800 in the company. Perhaps you are the director, perhaps according to the schedules you got a bit more, but what then exactly was invented and what exactly was fabricated --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that was used to damage your reputation?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was claimed that I did not distribute shares to everyone but just gave them to a group of close friends and kept some myself and left nothing to the employees, and that of course was a lie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, at least I understand what the criticism was. Why did you go to Mr. Karadzic to discuss these matters with him?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it yesterday. Some friends suggested that I should get in touch with him in the sense that Mr. Karadzic or the Serb Democratic Party could talk to those people who were attacking me and try and put a stop to it and make sure that this problem did not happen again in terms of somehow balancing things out with the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say it was all a fabrication. How was this distribution of shares registered, recorded? I mean, someone must have written down who now are the owners, you say approximately all of the 800. Where was that registered?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the company's books. And at the Industrial Tribunal as well. And everything was fine then and years later. There was no dispute ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for answering those questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Bench has no further questions. Do the questions of the Bench raise any need to put further questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I hope it will be a short one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, were any of these allegations about your part in the privatisation of the company, were they made at any time on television?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allusions to that topic, yes, and it was at the meeting of the Presidency, of the BH Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And so who were the individuals, if you can remember, who were making those allusions on television, or who did make those allusions on television?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic and Mr. Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there anybody from the Serb leadership who appeared on television on those same occasions that Mr. Kljuic or Mr. Izetbegovic appeared on television?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic were present, but they made no comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Antic, this concludes your testimony in this court. I would like to thank you very much for -- first of all for coming to The Hague, and of course for answering questions of both parties and of the Bench, and I wish you a safe trip home again. Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could go through the exhibits of this witness, but we'll need the assistance of the registrar. Perhaps since not all the documents are used, I'll read them out slowly. P979, guidelines on tasks, mode of action and functioning of defence forces, et cetera. P980, tape recording -- yes, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, but the first document here is just not valid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would tell Mr. Stewart why you consider it to be invalid, and then he can raise the objection in legal technical terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we don't pursue any objection to that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's 979. Perhaps, Your Honour, just to clarify what's going on, why there seems to be some consternation and possibly to, without making submissions, reassure Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Krajisnik has some things to say about this document. I'll put it as neutrally as that. When he comes to give evidence, he can say those things, but, Your Honour, his legal -- his lawyer's assessment is that it doesn't constitution an objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got no idea, Mr. Krajisnik, what you would like to say about it, but admission into evidence of this document doesn't mean that it ever enters into force, that it was -- if it's not signed, that it would have been a draft that was later changed. A lot of things can happen to a document. And if there would be any suggestion that it would have been forgery, so manufactured, and that it is not produced at that time but last year, then of course we would like to know about that because we would then invite Mr. Margetts to give further details as to the source of that document. Yes, Mr. Krajisnik, you would like to add something?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document was drafted by the government and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to invite my client through Your Honours not to do this. Your Honour, let me say with the utmost respect Your Honour's summary, the Defence lawyers, with respect, regard as entirely accurate and we hope that will constitute a reassurance to Mr. Krajisnik that such issues lie in the future and remain open for exploration, but Your Honour, I, please, would like to discourage my client from entering into this legal debate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you started to explain some matters about these documents which I take it, although we hardly heard anything of you, means that you have some knowledge of the background of this document. I don't know how you gained that knowledge or not, but since you are on the list of those who are to testify, you will be in a position to -- if questions are put to you, that you explain to us in detail everything about this. The problem is that if we would let you proceed at this moment, it would be a statement not given after you had given a solemn declaration, and therefore it would be totally unclear for us what to do at this moment with your comments on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore, please be aware that admission into evidence, we invited the Defence, and that was well understood, I take it -- understood by Mr. Stewart, that if there would be any authenticity issue or something like that, that we'd like to know that right away. If it's a matter of disputing the relevance, the binding force, the origin, the whatever else, we will hear that at the appropriate time. And we can't receive those comments at this moment because it would -- not from you as an accused. If you would like to bring to the attention of the Chamber, as now and then happens when I ask Mr. Margetts what he knows about the document, where it was -- if there's any such comment which is not evidence but just to first lead to see whether any evidence would be needed to better understand the document, then we'll hear from counsel. Then back to the list. P980, tape recording of the 64th session of the Presidency. And the translation. P981 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, apology for interrupting. The translation at this stage is a partial translation. We do intend to obtain the full translation in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it there already or should it be made? I've forgotten about the length of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Only the partial translation is with the document at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, would the Defence be in a position to tell us whether, apart from what the Prosecution considers to be the most relevant portions of this document, whether there would be any need for further translation, because it involves quite a lot of costs, and if no one asks for it, then we could save those costs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we -- we're not in a position to do that right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course Your Honour is not expecting that, but we take the point and Your Honour has in mind to leave it with us now to ask whether we wish anything further to be translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means that if we would take a decision on the admission today, then the -- let's take it very practical, then the Defence is invited to come back to the Chamber if more translation would be needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. It looks -- the document seems to be 23 pages long, as far as one can see, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know how much it takes, but -- a page takes for translation takes quite some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, indeed, Your Honour. Yes, we certainly -- Mr. Karganovic, more than anybody else, knows that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that, there's more time available to translate newly arrived documents that are awaiting translation. Okay, let's see. We hear from the Defence. Then we have P982, contract between the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Boksit company Milici. Next one, P983, speech of Momcilo Krajisnik in the Assembly of the Serbian People, February 1992. P984, intercepted -- an hour is missing, Mr. Registrar, a conversation between Momcilo Krajisnik and Radovan Karadzic, February 1992. P984 -- 985, decree on mandatory delivery of war booty, et cetera. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then all these documents are admitted into evidence and the Defence is entitled to ask for more translation of P981 -- no, it's not P981. It's P9 -- P980. Then there's one exhibit remaining from the witness Djordjevic. Mr. Registrar, no number has yet been assigned to that document. It's map of Foca not marked by the witness; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It wasn't given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please give us the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be, Your Honours, P986.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Not that it matters in the slightest, but it was a Defence exhibit. It doesn't matter, I suppose, because no doubt the Chamber will treat them both equally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. It even has the advantage that we don't have to disturb the numbering with jumping from Djordjevic to the next witness and jumping back to Djordjevic. So Mr. Registrar, a D number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D91, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D91 is the number of the map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And P986 remains free, available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D986 then, it's available for the next Prosecution Exhibit, yes. It should be P986.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and P986 was the number that would be conveniently assigned to the list of members of Novi Privrednik should the Defence be -- and the Trial Chamber be content for that to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps, Mr. Stewart, could you make up your mind already on whether it's worth at all to give it a number and then perhaps review the list and let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, perhaps we could just ask Mr. Margetts to explain the relevance of the document and why the Prosecution want it admitted and then we could make a decision here and now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I give it a guess just to see whether I -- I can imagine that this a first step in establishing who actually were the shareholders or member of Novi Privrednik. I also can imagine that some relevance is given to this document in relation to the answer the witness gave to the question whether it was just SDS members or also others who could become members and his answers to the question that he didn't remember any of the names and -- well, I'm just guessing. I have not looked at the list, but if his wife would be on that list, it might be a surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would you give us a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, we have no objection; it's clearly admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P986 is a list, undated, which bears the names of Privrednik shareholders. That's at least what I understand from the top, Mr. Josse. If there would be any objection against the description I just gave, then -- because it's not translated yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's not yet admitted because it still waits for translation to be admitted. I also wonder there if we don't pay any attention to all the names. It's a long list. Whether -- I take it that the Prosecution wants to draw our attention to some names or -- I mean, to have a list of hundred names of people we don't know, of course we might decipher some of the -- well, of the names we are familiar with, but again here, pages, pages are to be translated, where for me at this moment most important is to see what's on top of that list, what it presents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In Your Honour's characterisation of the relevance of the list, I can indicate that it was a first step and it may be the case that there is some additional explanation for who these people in fact are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. I take it -- do you need a full written translation in order to further orient yourself or would the title do? Because I would suggest under those circumstances that if there are specific names you'd like to draw our attention to, that you ask name 46 to be translated, 76, and other names, not -- and similarly, if the Defence would like to demonstrate that these were not SDS members but that perhaps the Queen of England is on the list or the president of the French Republic, that they should point at certain names as well which they consider relevant for us to understand the list better.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I would be surprised if some of these people named were on the list. Nevertheless, because the nature of the witness's answer, I think at this stage we consider it necessary to translate all of the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All right. Take that effort and we'll then -- we'll then give a decision on admission once the translation is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If Her Majesty is on the list, then as one of her counsel, I shall have something to say about the matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. Let's first see whether her name, if at all, will be highlighted by the Prosecution. Any further matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll adjourn until tomorrow afternoon, quarter past two, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 9th day of November, 2005, at 2.15 p.m. 24 25
